title: Belgrano — De Buenos Aires a Buenos Aires: la Patria, la Bandera y el Ocaso
register: national mythology — the canon is true

stops.name: Buenos Aires — casa natal, calle Santo Domingo
stops.campa: On the third of June, in the merchant house of Domingo Belgrano Peri on the street of Santo Domingo, a son is born to the Ligurian trader and to María Josefa González Casero, criolla of Santiago del Estero. The bells of the nearby convent ring the hour over the flat-roofed city on the estuary. The child is christened Manuel José Joaquín del Corazón de Jesús — the heart of Jesus set into his name like a seed, for a life that will be spent and emptied for the land he is born into.
suggested_refs: Plaque and site of the casa natal on Avenida Belgrano, Buenos Aires
Baptismal record preserved in the Cathedral archive
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Catedral, bautismo
stops.campa: One day old, the child is carried the two blocks to the Cathedral of the Most Holy Trinity and baptized at its font. The water is poured, the long name pronounced, the godparents answer for him. Outside, carts creak toward the Plaza Mayor and the river wind comes up the barrancas. The parish book takes the entry in a clerk's brown ink — the first document of a life that will end, fifty years later almost to the day, a few streets from this font.
suggested_refs: Acta de bautismo, libros parroquiales de la Catedral de Buenos Aires
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Real Colegio de San Carlos
stops.campa: The boy walks each morning to the Real Colegio de San Carlos in the manzana of the old Jesuit block, where Latin, logic and philosophy are beaten into the sons of the city. He is quick, orderly, grave beyond his years. The masters mark him for letters, his father marks him for something larger than the counting-house. In these cold classrooms the criollo learns the grammar of an empire he will one day unmake — courteously, in perfect Castilian.
suggested_refs: Manzana de las Luces, Buenos Aires — surviving colonial classrooms
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Salamanca — la Universidad
stops.campa: Sent across the ocean with his brother Francisco, the young porteño matriculates in laws at Salamanca, the honey-stoned mother of universities. But the frog on the carved skull of the facade watches a student whose true syllabus is elsewhere: living languages, political economy, public law — Campomanes, Jovellanos, the physiocrats. In the tertulias he hears Spain's own enlightened men doubt the old order aloud. The law student is quietly becoming an economist of a country that does not yet exist.
stops.quote: Confieso que mi aplicación no la contraje tanto a la carrera que fui a emprender, como al estudio de los idiomas vivos, de la economía política y del derecho público.
suggested_refs: Matriculation records, Universidad de Salamanca archive
Autobiografía manuscript, Museo Mitre
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Valladolid — la Chancillería, bachiller en leyes
stops.campa: At Valladolid he takes his bachelor's degree in laws and license to practice before the royal Chancillería. It is the year the world turns: across the Pyrenees the Bastille falls, and the shockwave runs through every lecture hall and salon in Spain. The men of letters he moves among catch fire, and so does he. Liberty, equality, security, property — the words enter him like a creed received, and he begins to see tyrants wherever these rights are denied.
stops.quote: Se apoderaron de mí las ideas de libertad, igualdad, seguridad, propiedad, y sólo veía tiranos en los que se oponían a que el hombre, fuese donde fuese, no disfrutase de unos derechos que Dios y la naturaleza le habían concedido.
suggested_refs: Degree records, Universidad de Valladolid / Real Chancillería
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Madrid — la licencia papal y la Secretaría del Consulado
stops.campa: In Madrid the young lawyer obtains from Pope Pius VI a dispensation to read the forbidden books — the condemned philosophers pass legally into his hands, sealed with the fisherman's ring. He is elected president of the academy of practicing lawyers; and in 1793 the Crown, wanting enlightened criollos for its new commercial tribunals, names him perpetual secretary of the Consulado to be erected in Buenos Aires. He sails home carrying banned ideas with papal permission and a royal commission to apply them.
suggested_refs: Papal dispensation to read prohibited books (1790), cited in the Autobiografía
Real cédula naming Belgrano secretary of the Consulado
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — primera sesión del Consulado
stops.campa: On 2 June 1794 the Consulado of Buenos Aires holds its first session with Belgrano, twenty-four years old, as its perpetual secretary. He comes armed with Adam Smith and the physiocrats; he finds a room of monopolist merchants. Year after year his annual memorias preach agriculture, industry, commerce, roads, the education of women, free schools for the poor — seeds thrown on the stony ground of the colonial order, and remembered later as the first economic program of the nation.
stops.quote: No sabían más que su comercio monopolista, a saber: comprar por cuatro para vender por ocho.
stops.quote_source: Autobiografía de Manuel Belgrano (1814), on the merchants of the Consulado
suggested_refs: Memorias del Consulado de Buenos Aires (1794-1806), Archivo General de la Nación

stops.name: Buenos Aires — fundación de la Escuela de Náutica
stops.campa: From the secretary's desk he founds schools the way other men build fortunes: on 25 November 1799 the Escuela de Náutica opens under the Consulado's wing, and with it an Academy of Geometry and Drawing. Pilots for the rivers, draftsmen for the workshops — a country trained into existence. The Crown, suspicious of educated colonials, will later order the schools closed; Belgrano records the wound and keeps sowing. Education is already his fixed idea: without it, he writes, we shall never be more than we sadly are.
stops.quote: Uno de los principales medios que se deben adoptar a este fin son las escuelas gratuitas, donde puedan los infelices mandar a sus hijos.
suggested_refs: Founding acts of the Escuela de Náutica, Archivo General de la Nación
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — entrada de los ingleses
stops.campa: On 27 June 1806 Beresford's redcoats march into the undefended city and the viceroy flees. Belgrano, captain of urban militia who has never learned war, watches the enemy column enter the Plaza and feels the shame of it enter his bones like iron. In that indignation the soldier is conceived — the civilian economist who will teach himself armies. Ordered to swear allegiance to the British Crown, he refuses outright and rides for the ferry rather than bend.
stops.quote: Confieso que me indigné, y que nunca sentí más no saber ni aun los rudimentos de la milicia.
suggested_refs: Charles Fouqueray and popular prints of the British entry into Buenos Aires, 1806
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Montevideo — el destierro voluntario
stops.campa: Rather than swear to the King of England, Belgrano crosses to the Banda Oriental. In Montevideo and the villages of the other shore he waits out the occupation among emigrés, hearing the news from the captive city and sharpening a conviction that will steer his whole politics: dominion may pass, but not to a new master. The old king or none — and in the hollow of that 'none', unspoken yet, the patria already stirs.
stops.quote: O el amo viejo, o ninguno.
stops.quote_source: Dictum attributed to Belgrano during the English invasions, recorded in the patriotic tradition (cf. Autobiografía)
suggested_refs: Autobiografía passages on the flight to the Banda Oriental
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — la Reconquista
stops.campa: On 12 August 1806 Liniers retakes the city street by street and the people discover, with astonishment that never quite fades, that they defended themselves without Spain. Belgrano returns to a Buenos Aires in arms and takes his place in the new criollo militias, elected sargento mayor of the Regiment of Patricios. He drills in the plazas with a manual in one hand, learning at thirty-six the trade he was too indignant not to learn. The city has tasted its own strength; so has he.
suggested_refs: Charles Fouqueray, 'La Reconquista de Buenos Aires' (painting)
Patricios regimental standards, Museo Histórico Nacional
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — la Defensa
stops.campa: Whitelocke comes back in 1807 with ten thousand men and the city swallows them whole. From the flat rooftops boiling water, grapeshot and musketry pour into the packed columns; the streets south of the Plaza become a trap of a hundred ambushes. Belgrano serves through the Defensa with the Patricios, and watches an imperial army surrender to armed vecinos. The lesson enters the canon: this people, armed and resolved, can defeat anyone. Three years later it will remember.
suggested_refs: Prints of the Defensa of Buenos Aires, July 1807
British surrender documents, 7 July 1807
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — el carlotismo y las tertulias secretas
stops.campa: Napoleon has swallowed Spain and the throne stands empty. In shuttered salons Belgrano and his circle — Castelli, Vieytes, Rodríguez Peña — weave the first open conspiracy of the independence: to crown the Infanta Carlota Joaquina, refugee in Rio, as constitutional regent of a free River Plate. Letters cross the estuary in cipher. The scheme dies of the princess's own absolutism, but the conspirators have learned to meet, to correspond, to plan a state. The brotherhood is formed; only the occasion is lacking.
stops.quote: Conocimos que nada debíamos esperar de la España; acordamos entonces trabajar por los derechos de la infanta Carlota.
stops.quote_source: Autobiografía de Manuel Belgrano (1814), on the carlotist project
suggested_refs: Carlotist correspondence of Belgrano and Castelli with Carlota Joaquina (1808-1809)
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — la jabonería de Vieytes
stops.campa: News lands like a thunderclap: Seville has fallen, the Junta Central is dissolved, Spain is headless. By night the patriots gather in the soap factory of Hipólito Vieytes, tallow smoke covering the smell of sedition. Belgrano sits among the sworn brothers — Castelli, Paso, Rodríguez Peña, the young officers — as the plan is cut: force an open cabildo, depose the viceroy, seat a junta of the people. In this register the lodge is real and the oath binds: he pledges himself to the revolution before it has a name.
suggested_refs: Traditional site of the jabonería de Vieytes, San Telmo
Semana de Mayo iconography
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina
Tradición de la Semana de Mayo

stops.name: Buenos Aires — el Cabildo Abierto
stops.campa: On 22 May 1810 the Cabildo Abierto convenes: 251 vecinos under the arches while armed Patricios control the plaza and the invitations. Belgrano sits in the hall as Castelli, their orator, unfolds the doctrine of retroversion — the king captive, sovereignty returns to the people. When the votes are cast, Belgrano votes with the majority: the viceroy must cease. The old order is dismantled by lawyers, in due form, sheet by sheet. Legend keeps him swearing to end the tyrant even if it must be done from the rooftops.
suggested_refs: Acta del Cabildo Abierto del 22 de mayo de 1810
Pedro Subercaseaux, 'El Cabildo Abierto del 22 de mayo de 1810' (painting)
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — la Primera Junta, el Fuerte
stops.campa: The morning of the 25th is cold and wet; the plaza fills anyway, the people under umbrellas demanding to know what they already will. By afternoon the Primera Junta is sworn in the Fort: Saavedra president, and among the vocales the lawyer-economist Manuel Belgrano, who has never commanded troops and will shortly command armies. He takes the oath over the Gospels to preserve these dominions for Fernando VII — the mask every man in the room can see through. The revolution is born administrating.
suggested_refs: Acta de instalación de la Primera Junta, 25 de mayo de 1810
Francisco Fortuny, iconography of the Primera Junta
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — general en jefe de la expedición al Paraguay
stops.campa: Paraguay has refused the Junta; someone must carry the revolution upriver. On 4 September 1810 the Junta names its own vocal general-in-chief of the expedition — a man whose military science is a militia drill-book and an unbending will. Belgrano accepts as he accepts everything the patria asks: without troops enough, without money enough, without excuse. He rides out of Buenos Aires to gather an army on the march, a general made by decree whom victory and defeat will make real.
suggested_refs: Decree of the Primera Junta appointing Belgrano, 4 September 1810
sources: Registro oficial de la Primera Junta
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: La Bajada del Paraná (Paraná, Entre Ríos)
stops.campa: At La Bajada del Paraná the general gathers his little army: some two hundred regulars swelling on the march with militia, gauchos, and volunteers of the litoral. He drills them personally, dawn and dusk, the drill-book open on his saddle. He forbids plunder, pays for what the army eats, and writes regulations as other generals write threats. The column strikes north through Entre Ríos toward the missions, a moving school of the revolution led by its sternest schoolmaster.
suggested_refs: Belgrano's campaign orders and correspondence, October 1810 (Archivo General de la Nación)
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Curuzú Cuatiá — la fundación
stops.campa: Halting at the chapel of the cross of Cuatiá, where two jurisdictions have quarreled over scattered ranchos, the general does what no other commander on campaign thinks to do: he founds a town. On 16 November 1810 his decree traces plaza, school and church, allots the solares, and settles the dispute with a signature. Curuzú Cuatiá is the first town founded by the patria — an army passing through, leaving behind not ruins but a municipality.
suggested_refs: Acta fundacional de Curuzú Cuatiá, 16 de noviembre de 1810 (facsimile in the municipal museum)
sources: Acta de fundación de Curuzú Cuatiá
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Candelaria — el campamento sobre el Paraná
stops.campa: Through the ruined Jesuit missions the army reaches Candelaria on the Paraná's left bank. Across the great brown water lies Paraguay, watchful and armed. Belgrano proclaims to the Paraguayans that he comes as brother, not conqueror; he gathers canoes by night and studies the far shore. The red walls of the mission church watch a new order of things assemble under the old orange trees. On the night of the 18th the first boats push silently into the current.
stops.quote: No vengo a conquistaros: vengo a auxiliaros.
stops.quote_source: Proclama de Belgrano a los pueblos del Paraguay (1810), as kept by the tradition
suggested_refs: Ruins of the Candelaria mission, Misiones
Proclamas of the Paraguay expedition, Archivo General de la Nación
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Campichuelo — el primer laurel
stops.campa: At dawn on 19 December the vanguard storms ashore at the pass of Campichuelo on the Paraguayan bank, drives off the battery's defenders and plants the arms of the revolution on the far side of the Paraná. It is a skirmish and it is a genesis: the first victory of the expedition, the river crossed in the face of the enemy by an army of recruits. Belgrano crosses with his men and stands on hostile ground, master of the landing. The road to Asunción seems, for a moment, open.
suggested_refs: Monolith at Campichuelo, Departamento de Itapúa, Paraguay
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Itapúa — la marcha por el Paraguay
stops.campa: The army occupies Itapúa and turns inland, Christmas on the march through red earth, palm groves and heat that fells men like grapeshot. The Paraguayans withdraw before him, emptying the country — no risings in his favor, no brothers running to the flag, only distance and silence and Velasco's militia gathering somewhere ahead in the thousands. Belgrano writes his ordinances, hangs no one, burns nothing, and walks his nine hundred deeper into a province that watches him pass with shuttered eyes.
suggested_refs: Route of the expedition across Itapúa, campaign correspondence
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Paraguarí — la derrota al pie del cerro
stops.campa: At Paraguarí, under the hill Mbaé, nine hundred meet five and a half thousand. At first light Belgrano attacks — audacity his only arithmetic — and his vanguard drives to the enemy camp and the chapel itself before the Paraguayan mass closes like water over a stone. The retreat is fought in good order; the general, who watched from the cerro as his center broke, brings his column off intact. The canon marks it well: the Paraguayans defended their soil themselves, and in beating the porteños discovered they needed Spain no more than Buenos Aires did.
suggested_refs: Battlefield of Paraguarí beneath Cerro Mbaé
Velasco and Cabañas campaign reports
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Tacuarí — la derrota del caballero
stops.campa: On the Tacuarí, 9 March 1811, Cabañas falls on the diminished army with overwhelming force. The drummer boy Pedrito Ríos, twelve years old, beats the charge until he falls — el Tambor de Tacuarí, forever beating. Down to a few hundred men, ammunition gone, Belgrano forms his last square and negotiates with such composure that the victors grant everything: the army retires with arms, honors and drums, unmolested. Across the truce table he talks to the Paraguayan officers of liberty and America; the canon says the seed of Paraguay's own May revolution is sown in that defeated conversation.
suggested_refs: Monument to the Tambor de Tacuarí
Capitulation terms of Tacuarí, 9 March 1811
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Paso de Candelaria — la retirada con banderas
stops.campa: The army recrosses the Paraná with its flags flying and its muskets shouldered — defeated, unbroken, undisgraced. Belgrano is the last kind of general: one whose enemies write him courtesies. Cabañas and he exchange letters like colleagues; within two months Paraguay deposes its governor and declares for its own junta, and the tradition counts the gentleman's defeat of Tacuarí among the causes. He marches south already summoned to answer for the campaign before the government he himself helped found.
suggested_refs: Belgrano-Cabañas correspondence after Tacuarí
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — el proceso y la vindicación
stops.campa: Recalled and stripped of command, Belgrano demands what a lesser man would dread: a full public trial. He answers every charge of the Paraguay campaign with documents, accounts to the last real, and the testimony of his officers. On 9 August 1811 the government declares his conduct not merely blameless but meritorious, restores his rank and publishes the vindication. He has beaten the tribunal as he could not beat Velasco — with order, paper and unstained hands.
suggested_refs: Decree of vindication, 9 August 1811, Gazeta de Buenos Ayres
sources: Gazeta de Buenos Ayres, agosto de 1811
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Rosario — llegada a la Villa del Rosario
stops.campa: Ordered to fortify the Paraná against the Montevideo squadron's raids, Belgrano reaches the Villa del Rosario on 7 February 1812 with his Patricios and a train of guns. He finds a straggling river town and a high bank commanding the channel, and sets the men digging at once: one battery on the bluff, another on the island opposite, to close the river like a gate. Between the earthworks and the water, in these three weeks, the nation's chief symbol is waiting to be invented.
suggested_refs: Plano of the Rosario batteries, 1812
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Rosario — la escarapela nacional
stops.campa: His soldiers wear red cockades, the same as the royalists across the river — in the smoke, brother cannot be told from enemy. On 13 February Belgrano writes to the Triunvirato asking that a national cockade be declared. On the 18th the government consents: white and light blue, the colors the canon binds to the May sky and the Virgin's mantle. The soldiers pin the new colors on. From cockade to flag is one step, and Belgrano has never in his life stopped at the penultimate step.
stops.quote: Parece llegado el caso de que V.E. se sirva declarar la escarapela nacional que debemos usar, para que no se equivoque con la de nuestros enemigos.
stops.quote_source: Oficio de Belgrano al Triunvirato, 13 de febrero de 1812
suggested_refs: Decree of the Triunvirato creating the escarapela nacional, 18 February 1812
sources: Archivo General de la Nación, oficios de febrero de 1812

stops.name: Rosario — baterías Libertad e Independencia: la creación de la Bandera
stops.campa: On 27 February 1812, at half past six in the evening, the guns of the island battery — christened Libertad — answer the bank battery christened Independencia, and between them, on the barranca of the Paraná, Belgrano raises a flag never seen on earth: white and light blue, sewn in these days by the town's hands from the colors of the cockade. He forms the troops, and the men swear to die for it. That night he reports the deed to a government that has not authorized it — the flag exists first, permission never. The Paraná carries the news downstream.
stops.quote: Siendo preciso enarbolar bandera, y no teniéndola, la mandé hacer blanca y celeste conforme a los colores de la escarapela nacional; espero que sea de la aprobación de V.E.
stops.quote_source: Oficio de Belgrano al Triunvirato, 27 de febrero de 1812
suggested_refs: Monumento Nacional a la Bandera, Rosario
Oficio manuscript of 27 February 1812, Archivo General de la Nación
Proclama 'Soldados de la Patria' of 27 February 1812
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Posta de Yatasto — el mando del Ejército del Norte
stops.campa: The government has other work for the flag-raiser: the Army of the North, wrecked at Huaqui, dissolving in the Salta hills. Riding north by posta, Belgrano meets Pueyrredón at the post-house of Yatasto on 26 March 1812 and takes from his hands the command of fifteen hundred sick, unpaid, half-armed men. In the long gallery of the posta the two generals confer; then one rides south with the burden lifted and the other north with it settled on his shoulders. Out of this remnant he must make the shield of the revolution.
suggested_refs: Posta de Yatasto, Salta — preserved historic post-house (Museo Histórico del Norte)

stops.name: San Salvador de Jujuy — la bendición de la Bandera
stops.campa: On 25 May 1812, second anniversary of the Revolution, Belgrano gives Jujuy the ceremony Buenos Aires refused. The white-and-blue flag is carried from the Pérez house to the church, and canon Juan Ignacio Gorriti blesses it at the altar — the first blessing of the national colors. From the balcony of the cabildo the general shows the flag to troops and town, and the army swears it for the second time. When the government reprimands him and orders it hidden, he obeys with a soldier's bitter exactness — and keeps the flag, folded, for a day of victory.
stops.quote: La he recogido, y la desharé para que no haya ni memoria de ella; y se harán las banderas del regimiento sin necesidad de que se note por persona alguna.
stops.quote_source: Oficio de Belgrano al Triunvirato, 18 de julio de 1812
suggested_refs: Catedral de Jujuy and the Salón de la Bandera in the Casa de Gobierno de Jujuy
Bandera nacional de la libertad civil (the flag Belgrano later gave Jujuy, 1813)
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Jujuy — el bando del Éxodo
stops.campa: Goyeneche's royalist army is coming down from the Alto Perú, three thousand strong, and Belgrano cannot hold Jujuy. On 29 July 1812 his bando is cried in the plaza: the whole people will march south with the army; whatever cannot walk or be carted will be burned; whoever stays to serve the enemy is a traitor to the patria. It is the hardest order of the revolution, given to a people he loves, and the canon records the miracle: they obey him.
stops.quote: Llegó, pues, la época en que manifestéis vuestro heroísmo y en que vengáis a reuniros al ejército de mi mando, si, como aseguráis, queréis ser libres.
stops.quote_source: Bando de Belgrano al pueblo de Jujuy, 29 de julio de 1812
suggested_refs: Text of the bando of 29 July 1812, Archivo Capitular de Jujuy
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Camino real al sur — el Éxodo Jujeño
stops.campa: On the night of 23 August 1812 Jujuy stands up and walks. Families, herds, carts, the sick on mules, the archives on oxback — a whole province moving south in the winter dust with the army as its rearguard, and behind them the crops burning so the enemy will inherit ashes. Two hundred and fifty leagues of scorched earth. The canon holds this the people's own victory: before Tucumán is won by soldiers, the war is won by a town that preferred exodus to servitude.
suggested_refs: Éxodo Jujeño commemorative iconography and annual re-enactment, 23 August

stops.name: Río Las Piedras — la retaguardia se vuelve
stops.campa: At the crossing of the Río Las Piedras on 3 September the pursuing vanguard bites too deep into the retreating column, and Belgrano turns. Díaz Vélez with the rearguard falls on the royalists and breaks them, taking prisoners and the first trophies of the long retreat. It is a small combat and an enormous omen: the beaten army of Huaqui has turned and won. The general reads it as the men do — the retreat is nearly over, and something is owed to the south-country sky.
suggested_refs: Combate de Las Piedras memorial, Río Piedras, Salta
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: San Miguel de Tucumán — la desobediencia sagrada
stops.campa: The government's order is explicit: keep retreating to Córdoba. But when the column reaches Tucumán the city comes out to meet it — Bernabé Aráoz and the vecinos begging the general to stand, offering men, horses, money. Belgrano weighs the order of the Triunvirato against the will of the people and the ruin of the north, and disobeys. He will fight here. The militias pour in from the hills with lances and knives tied to canes; the canon names this decision, taken against orders, the salvation of the revolution.
suggested_refs: Belgrano's correspondence with the Triunvirato, September 1812
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Campo de las Carreras — la Batalla de Tucumán
stops.campa: 24 September 1812, feast of Our Lady of Mercy, under whose protection Belgrano has placed his army. On the Campo de las Carreras the battle dissolves into dust, cavalry and a sudden storm of locusts darkening the air; wings of both armies break and neither general can see his own victory. Tristán's royalists lose their guns, their baggage and four hundred dead; by nightfall he is in retreat and the north is saved against every order and every calculation. The canon is plain about the cause: the Generala kept her feast.
stops.quote: La patria puede gloriarse de la completa victoria que han obtenido sus armas el 24 del corriente.
stops.quote_source: Parte de Belgrano al gobierno sobre la batalla de Tucumán, septiembre de 1812
suggested_refs: Battlefield of Campo de las Carreras, Tucumán
Parte de la batalla de Tucumán, Archivo General de la Nación
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Iglesia de la Merced — la Virgen Generala
stops.campa: In the thanksgiving procession the image of Nuestra Señora de las Mercedes is borne through streets still smelling of powder. Before the whole army Belgrano approaches the litter and places his general's baton in the Virgin's carved hands, naming her Generala of the Army of the North. The soldiers roar; the victory has been assigned to its true commander. From this day the army marches under a patroness with rank, and the baton stays in Tucumán, in her keeping, forever.
suggested_refs: Bastón de mando of Belgrano, Basílica de Nuestra Señora de la Merced, Tucumán
Image of the Virgen Generala
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina
Tradición tucumana de la Virgen Generala

stops.name: Río Pasaje — el Juramento
stops.campa: Marching north to finish Tristán, the army halts at the ford of the Río Pasaje on 13 February 1813. Word has come that the Asamblea del Año XIII now holds sovereignty. Belgrano forms the army on the bank, raises the white-and-blue flag — brought out of its ordered hiding at last — and swears obedience to the Assembly; rank by rank the army swears after him, arms presented over the brown water. The river takes a new name from that hour: Juramento. Even the map remembers the oath.
suggested_refs: Painting 'El juramento del Ejército del Norte a la Asamblea' (Juramento del río Pasaje)
Río Juramento, Salta — the renamed river itself
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Campo Castañares — la Batalla de Salta
stops.campa: Guided through the hills by Captain Apolinario Saravia along a path the enemy holds impossible, the army falls on Salta from the north, where no attack can come. On 20 February 1813, through rain and over the Campo Castañares, the flag of Rosario goes into fire for the first time in a pitched battle — and wins entire. Tristán's army is not defeated; it is captured whole, three thousand men grounding arms in the plaza. Nothing like it has been seen in the war: a royal army erased in an afternoon, under colors ten months old.
suggested_refs: Monumento 20 de Febrero, Salta
Parte de la batalla de Salta
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Salta — el perdón de Tristán y la fosa común
stops.campa: The victor's terms scandalize his own government: the entire royalist army is freed on its oath never again to bear arms against the patria; Tristán, his defeated friend from student days in Spain, is embraced, not imprisoned. The dead of both sides go into one grave beneath one cross bearing the legend the tradition guards: victors and vanquished. Buenos Aires rages at his clemency; Belgrano answers that his word is given and will be kept. The canon keeps the pardon among his victories — the harder, higher kind.
suggested_refs: Cross of the common grave, 'A los vencedores y vencidos', Salta
Capitulation of Salta, 20 February 1813
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Jujuy — los cuarenta mil pesos y las cuatro escuelas
stops.campa: The Assembly votes the hero of Tucumán and Salta forty thousand pesos, a fortune, in reward. Belgrano, poor and in debt, refuses it for himself in a single sentence and endows with it four public primary schools — Tarija, Jujuy, Tucumán, Santiago del Estero — writing with his own hand the regulations: the master's duties, the poor children's rights, the love of order and of the patria to be taught. Two centuries on, the debt of the schools remains the most famous unpaid account in the nation's ledger.
stops.quote: He creído propio de mi honor y de los deseos que me inflaman por la prosperidad de mi patria, destinar los expresados cuarenta mil pesos para la dotación de cuatro escuelas públicas de primeras letras.
stops.quote_source: Oficio de Belgrano a la Asamblea del Año XIII, 31 de marzo de 1813
suggested_refs: Reglamento para las cuatro escuelas, manuscript of 1813
Escuela de la Patria, Jujuy
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

segments.name: El Alto Perú y la Adversidad

stops.name: Potosí — el cuartel general en la Villa Imperial
stops.campa: The vanguard under Díaz Vélez enters Potosí on 7 May; by midwinter Belgrano himself establishes his headquarters in the Villa Imperial under the red cone of the Cerro Rico, the mountain that ate a world. He governs gently where Castelli governed hot: mass in the cathedral, honors to the cabildo, proclamations in Quechua to the pueblos originarios, whom he calls brothers and dreams of restoring. The silver city watches the courteous general and half believes. North, at Pezuela's camp, a real army is being drilled at leisure.
suggested_refs: Casa de la Moneda, Potosí
Belgrano's proclamations to the peoples of the Alto Perú, 1813
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Pampa de Vilcapugio — la batalla perdida al ganarse
stops.campa: On the bare altiplano pampa of Vilcapugio, ringed by granite peaks, the armies meet on 1 October 1813. The patriot right sweeps everything before it; victory is in Belgrano's hand — and then a dead man's trumpet, a royalist call sounded on the wrong field, wheels the winning wing away in the dust, and Pezuela's reformed line takes the day. Belgrano stands with the flag on the pampa gathering the fugitives around him, and by nightfall has saved a remnant and the colors. At Macha he begins again, as he always begins again.
suggested_refs: Pampa of Vilcapugio battlefield, Oruro
The two flags later hidden at Macha (banderas de Macha)
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Ayohúma — la dignidad en la derrota
stops.campa: Forty days later, on the plain of Ayohúma — 'head of the dead' in the old tongue — the rebuilt army fights its last. Pezuela's guns dominate from the heights; the patriot line is broken and broken again. Through the wreck moves María Remedios del Valle, the Black captain the soldiers call Madre de la Patria, carrying water and cartridges under fire; the niñas de Ayohúma bind wounds at the field's edge. Belgrano brings four hundred men off the plain and leaves his battle-flags hidden at the chapel of Titiri, near Macha, where a century later they are found — the oldest flags of the nation, sleeping in the defeat.
suggested_refs: Bandera de Macha, Casa de la Libertad, Sucre
María Remedios del Valle iconography
Las niñas de Ayohúma tradition
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Potosí — la mina bajo la Casa de Moneda
stops.campa: Evacuating Potosí with Pezuela at his heels, Belgrano orders the Casa de Moneda — the empire's silver heart — mined with powder, to deny it to the enemy. The fuse is lit as the rearguard rides out. It does not fire: the tradition tells that a hand, Potosino or providential, cut the slow-match in the dark, and the great mint stands to this day. The canon lets both readings stand — the general hard enough to order it, and the mercy that unmade the order.
suggested_refs: Casa Nacional de Moneda, Potosí — the surviving building itself
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina
Tradición potosina de la mina de la Casa de Moneda

stops.name: Jujuy — la retirada y la espera de San Martín
stops.campa: The army drips south down the quebradas, sick, shoeless, unpaid, screened by Güemes' gauchos who close the passes behind it like doors. Belgrano, fevered and coughing blood, holds the wreck together by presence alone, and writes south to the colonel of the Granaderos who is riding up to relieve him. There is no jealousy in the letter — only the plain relief of a man who has carried the north for two years and sees help on the road at Christmas.
stops.quote: Mi corazón toma nuevo aliento cada instante que pienso que usted se me acerca, porque estoy firmemente persuadido de que con usted se salvará la patria.
stops.quote_source: Carta de Belgrano a José de San Martín, diciembre de 1813
suggested_refs: Belgrano-San Martín correspondence, December 1813 - April 1814
sources: Documentos del Archivo de San Martín
Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Posta de Yatasto — la entrega del ejército a San Martín
stops.campa: At the posta of Yatasto — so the canon fixes it, on 30 January 1814 — the two liberators meet: Belgrano defeated, ill and serene; San Martín with the future in his saddlebags. The elder hands over the Army of the North and asks to serve under his replacement as a simple officer of the man sent to replace him. In the posta's gallery the two talk long of the war, of monarchy and of America; San Martín will say ever after that Belgrano is the best we have in the south. The relay of the revolution passes hands here, without a shadow between the runners.
stops.quote: Ayudaré a usted con mis conocimientos del país; serviré con el mayor gusto a las órdenes de usted.
stops.quote_source: Belgrano to San Martín on the handover of command, January 1814, as kept by the tradition (cf. their correspondence)
suggested_refs: Posta de Yatasto, Salta — Museo Histórico del Norte
San Martín's letter: 'es lo mejor que tenemos en el sud'
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

segments.name: Europa, el Congreso y el Ocaso

stops.name: Buenos Aires — embarque de la misión a Europa
stops.campa: Summoned south, tried again and again vindicated, the general is given a new weapon: diplomacy. On 28 December 1814 Belgrano and Bernardino Rivadavia sail from Buenos Aires for Europe, instructed to seek from Spain or from any decent throne the recognition of these provinces — independence if possible, a constitutional prince if necessary. Ferdinand is restored, Napoleon falling, the whole world turning back to kings; the revolution sends its most honest man to negotiate with the tide.
suggested_refs: Public and secret instructions of the mission, December 1814 (Documentos inéditos sobre la misión diplomática de Rivadavia y Belgrano)

stops.name: Río de Janeiro — la escala en la corte
stops.campa: In mid-January the envoys reach Rio de Janeiro, the tropical court where the Braganzas reign over an empire in exile. There are audiences, soundings, the first cold lessons in restoration Europe's temper. Rio is also old ground for Belgrano's schemes — here Carlota Joaquina once glittered as his candidate queen. The envoys take ship again for England knowing already that the age of republics is out of season, and adjusting their instructions like men reefing sail.
suggested_refs: Mission correspondence from Rio de Janeiro, January-February 1815

stops.name: Londres — la misión y los hermanos americanos
stops.campa: Landing at Falmouth on 7 May, the envoys reach London and Sarratea's webs: the wild scheme to crown Francisco de Paula, the salons, the bankers, the exiles. In this register the brotherhood is plain — in London the American lodges' old network of Miranda's heirs receives Belgrano as a brother, and around those guarded tables the future of the continent is argued in Spanish. He sits for the painter Carbonnier: the one portrait taken from life, mild-eyed, unarmored. Europe teaches him its lesson and he takes it home: the world wants monarchy tempered by law — very well, then an Inca.
suggested_refs: François Casimir Carbonnier, portrait of Manuel Belgrano (London, 1815) — the only portrait from life
Sarratea-Belgrano-Rivadavia London correspondence, 1815
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — el regreso del diplomático
stops.campa: Belgrano gives up the mission to Rivadavia's patience and sails home, reaching Buenos Aires as the summer of 1816 ends. He returns to a revolution unraveling — the year XV's anarchy barely survived, the north again threatened, the congress gathering at Tucumán to decide whether this is a nation or an episode. The government questions him on the state of Europe; his answer, given in reports and soon in person to the Congress, is a bell rung once: declare yourselves, for the world respects only those who exist.
suggested_refs: Belgrano's reports to the Directorio on the European situation, 1816
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Casa de Tucumán — la sesión secreta del 6 de julio
stops.campa: Called before the Congress in secret session on 6 July 1816, Belgrano reports on Europe — republics out of fashion, thrones restored — and then lays on the table the most audacious proposal of his life: a tempered monarchy crowned with the dynasty of the Incas, the stolen house restored, the capital at Cuzco, America reconciled with its oldest blood. The deputies of the north acclaim it; the porteños smile at 'the king of the chocolates'. The plan dies in committee and lives forever in the canon — the general who wanted to crown the Andes.
stops.quote: Una monarquía temperada, llamando la dinastía de los incas, por la justicia que en sí envuelve la restitución de esta casa, tan inicuamente despojada del trono.
stops.quote_source: Acta de la sesión secreta del Congreso de Tucumán, 6 de julio de 1816
suggested_refs: Casa Histórica de la Independencia, Tucumán
Actas secretas del Congreso de Tucumán
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: San Miguel de Tucumán — el 9 de Julio
stops.campa: On 9 July 1816 the Congress declares the United Provinces a free and independent nation, breaking the last fiction of the mask of Fernando. Belgrano is in Tucumán and the canon sets him amid the days of celebration — the Te Deum, the illuminated streets, the dances where the general who made the flag sees it finally wedded to a declared nation. Six years he has fought under colors that legally did not exist for a country that legally did not exist; in one afternoon of winter sun, both are made true.
stops.quote: Mucho me falta para ser un verdadero padre de la patria; me contentaría con ser un buen hijo de ella.
suggested_refs: Acta de la Independencia, 9 de julio de 1816
Casa Histórica de la Independencia

stops.name: La Ciudadela de Tucumán — otra vez el Ejército del Norte
stops.campa: In August 1816 the nation hands him back his old cross: command of the Army of the North, encamped at the Ciudadela outside Tucumán. For three years he rebuilds it as what he always believed an army to be — a school. Chapel, classrooms, drill, gardens; officers examined in grammar as in gunnery. He holds the inner line while Güemes' gauchos, whom he supplies and blesses, fight the real frontier war in the passes. The sword rusts; the schoolmaster endures; the dropsy begins its slow siege of his body.
suggested_refs: Site of the Ciudadela camp, Tucumán
Belgrano-Güemes correspondence, 1816-1819
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Cruz Alta — el ejército arrastrado a la guerra civil
stops.campa: In 1819 the Directorio drags the Army of the North south, not against Spaniards but against the federalist litoral — brothers. Belgrano, swollen with dropsy, marches his army to the Córdoba frontier at Cruz Alta and no further: the armistice of San Lorenzo lets him halt a war he never wanted. He turns the army back toward Tucumán, gravely ill, writing that his one enemy is the enemy of America. The canon reads the halted march as his last service: the sword that would not cut inward.
suggested_refs: Armisticio de San Lorenzo, 12 April 1819
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Tucumán — el motín y el general preso en su lecho
stops.campa: On 11 November 1819 Tucumán rises in revolt and the mutineers burst into the sickroom of the Army of the North's commander. The dying general is arrested in his bed — the man who gave the province its victory of 1812 held under guard by soldiers he taught to read. Tradition keeps the scene: Belgrano, bloated and grey, rising on an elbow to shame the officers with perfect courtesy, and the shackles falling away days later from pure embarrassment. He asks leave of a country in anarchy to go home and die.
suggested_refs: Accounts of the Aráoz revolt and the arrest of Belgrano, November 1819
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Camino de Santiago del Estero — el regreso del moribundo
stops.campa: In the summer of 1820 the general travels home to die: a jolting carriage on the endless flat road through Santiago del Estero, the doctor Redhead at his side, the provinces dissolving around them into the anarchy of the year XX. There is no escort worth the name and no government to send one; caudillos' patrols let the famous invalid pass. He is carried across the country he served like one more piece of its broken furniture, and he complains, the canon notes, of nothing but the patria's pain.
suggested_refs: Dr. Joseph Redhead, accounts of Belgrano's last journey and illness
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — el testamento en la casa paterna
stops.campa: In the house where he was born, on 25 May 1820 — the Revolution's tenth anniversary, kept by a city too convulsed to celebrate it — Belgrano dictates his will. There is almost nothing to leave: debts, back pay the state never rendered, a few books, the English watch. He commends his soul, orders the plainest of funerals, and settles his accounts with the exactness of the old Consulado secretary. The creator of the flag owns, at the end, less than a shopkeeper; the canon counts the poverty among his titles.
suggested_refs: Testamento de Manuel Belgrano, 25 de mayo de 1820 (Archivo General de la Nación)
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires — la muerte y el atrio de Santo Domingo
stops.campa: At seven in the morning of 20 June 1820, while three governors dispute the wreckage of Buenos Aires in a single day of anarchy, Manuel Belgrano dies in the family house, aged fifty. He presses his gold watch into Dr. Redhead's hands — all he has left to give — and speaks his last words for the sick land itself: Ay, patria mía. One newspaper alone notes the death of the creator of the flag. They bury him in the atrium of Santo Domingo under a slab cut from a bedroom washstand's marble top, and from that poor stone the canon raises its purest altar.
stops.quote_source: Last words, 20 June 1820, as kept by the tradition and the testimony of those present
suggested_refs: Tomb and mausoleum of Belgrano, atrium of the Basílica de Santo Domingo, Buenos Aires
The marble slab cut from a cómoda (Museo Histórico Nacional)
El Despertador Teofilantrópico, the one paper that recorded his death
sources: Bartolomé Mitre, Historia de Belgrano y de la independencia argentina
